utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-R77, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin concerning allegations against Milka Maglov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, Ms. Maglov. I want to make sure that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's perfect. Thank you. If there is any problem with interpretation at any time, please let me know, draw my attention immediately. Appearances amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Brenda J. Hollis, appearing as amicus curiae Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, ma'am. Appearances for the Defence, Ms. Jevtovic. So are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention something. We will be moving to Monday, as things look, and Monday we will have the witnesses for the Defence, remaining witnesses for the Defence for that matter. How do you wish to proceed after that? Because I do not consider these proceedings as complicated procedurally as the trial proceedings, the usual trial proceedings. I want to know whether you would accept or whether you are ready, after we conclude with the hearing of evidence on Monday, to make final submissions there and then, after which we then adjourn for judgement, or whether you would like time and submit pleadings -- final submissions in writing later on, in which case you also need to tell me whether you would be -- you would agree that these will not then be followed by oral submissions too, and that will be practically the end of it and we will deliver our judgement later on in due course, in any case, just the same. But I am going to leave this to you. I am leaving the options open without telling you what my preference is, and frankly, I haven't even discussed it with the other two Judges as yet, for a very simple reason, and I'm speaking out along these lines now so that you will have time to think about this. It may well be that after that the evidence has finished on Monday, you may require time to go through all the evidence, transcript, compare transcript and evidence here with prior statements and whatever, and that you would prefer to have some time to prepare final submissions in writing. I don't think that there would be difficulties there. I would certainly recommend to my two colleagues to accept that for sure, if such a request is forthcoming. If you prefer, on the other hand, you feel you are well prepared to make final submissions orally on Monday, or even on Tuesday, if you want, we can do that. Tuesday we have a sitting in the Brdjanin case. It's only one witness. It won't last long. I reckon it will only be in the region of about half an hour, not more than that. So you would -- you could actually have, theoretically speaking, anything like two and a half hours all for yourselves if you want to make final submissions. What I wouldn't like is to have oral submissions and then written submissions. That I think would be a waste of time. So think about it. I don't want the response now. It was just food for thought. And after the first break, please come back to us and tell us what your preferences are. All right? But we do not intend to follow with the system of final briefs and then go through those and then final submissions and we drag this on for another two, three, four months. I mean, it's a case which does not deserve that much formality. And anyway, I consider contempt proceedings, as I said, less formal than what we are briefed with here. Okay? Let's bring the witness in. Naturally, I also wanted that if there is anything in the Rules that applies mutatis mutandis to contempt proceedings that you insist on, then obviously we will consider that in terms of the Rules. I mean, I'm making myself clear, but I don't think it's the case of being too formalistic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ukropina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. We will be proceeding with your cross-examination, which I hope won't last too long, and which would make possible for you to leave this courtroom, and if you have any time left, enjoy a little bit of The Hague and the sun, which is out today, although it's cold. So please take a chair, take a seat. You are testifying on the basis of the same solemn declaration that you entered yesterday. Yes, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ukropina.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: I would like page 74, line 15 of the transcript shown. All right. In the transcript, it's on page 74, line 15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This was yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry. I'm talking to myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: You said Mr. Peric said explicitly that you did have the witness statement before you went to visit him and at the moment when you went to see him, you knew that he was a witness, a Prosecution witness. Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what the transcript says, I suppose it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: You don't have Mr. Peric's statement in front of you now, but my assistant can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page was it? Page 70 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 74, page 74, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 74, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will read out to the witness while you prepare the statement. Your answer was as follows, Mr. Ukropina: "Mr. Peric said quite explicitly that you did receive the witness statement before you went on your first visit, that at the moment when you went to see him, you knew that he was a witness, that he was a Prosecution witness." This is what he said. And then you were actually confronted with the witness statement. So we are back to that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are coming back to this statement, to page number 1. I underline -- I underlined the section that I would like the witness to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was only then that he told us, towards the end of the interview, that they had come to see him, and he gave a statement to somebody from the Tribunal. But he told them that he wouldn't like to testify, that he would like to build bridges of friendship. Until then, we didn't know that he had given statements to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and we then said goodbye to him and we exchanged calling cards."

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the witness if he could read slowly so that they can translate everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you follow, Mr. Jevtovic? Mr. Ukropina. My apologies to you, Ms. Jevtovic. Yes. Could you read it out again, please, and slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was only then that he told us, towards the end of the interview, that people had come to see him and that he had given a statement to somebody from the Tribunal. But that he wouldn't like to testify. Instead, he would like to build bridges of friendship. He would not like to testify. It was the first time we found out that he had given a statement to someone. Until then, we didn't know that he had given a statement to representatives of the Prosecution, and we had not received his statement. We said goodbye to him and exchanged calling cards."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Do you still stand by your yesterday's testimony?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, I misinterpreted it yesterday when I spoke about Mr. Peric's statement. Namely, during the process of investigation that I carried out in 2002, one of the problems I encountered was whether there was one visit to the witness or two. This statement of Mr. Peric's obviously refers to the alleged first visit about which the witness says that he never received it; instead, that he was visited only once, in September. That is, during that visit in December, both Mr. Peric and Mrs. Maglov said they were aware the witness had given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. So what Mr. Peric said is true, namely, that as to the first visit, there is no evidence that they had known that he was a witness during that first visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: You actually said something that is completely inaccurate. I am drawing your attention to the fact that everything you said just now is completely inaccurate. Can you please remember, since you are an investigator, other statements?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can recollect them. The witness explicitly speaks that there was only one visit in December. R77-B says that he visited the witness in September, together with you. He mentions only one visit to the -- the witness mentions only one visit in September, and he says that he doesn't know where you went when you left his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: If we can now come back for a moment to a section of yesterday's cross-examination. You said that we read, that is, reread, our own statements, Mr. Peric and I. If I tell you now that the statement that I signed was in front of me and I said: "All right. I know what I said." There were a lot of papers in B/C/S and in English, and I actually did not read anything before I signed.

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is absolutely not true. When I came for the second time to see you in Banja Luka, the statement was given to you in B/C/S and you took your time, at least 15 minutes, to read it in piece. Maybe you read it even twice. I don't know. In any case, it took some time. And finally, you said: "Yes, this is what I stated." You asked me where to sign, and I told you to sign on every page, including the last page, which is actually witness confirmation, stating that the witness is aware that the statement may be used before the court. At any rate, you read the whole statement, maybe even twice, and it took at least 15 minutes, the reading of your statement in B/C/S. Finally, when you signed, I gave you the English version of the text, explaining that this is the same identical text, translated into English. It is true that you didn't ask me to translate it again. You took my word for it that it was identical wording in English, and you signed the text in English as well. There were three statements in B/C/S, that is, three copies, plus three copies of the statement in English. I kept two originals, leaving one original of each to you, in English and in B/C/S. Absolutely the same procedure was followed with the taking and signing of the statement of Mr. Peric, just after I finished with you, with the proviso that while you were reading and signing your statement, Mr. Peric was out of the office and you left the office at the moment when he came in to read and sign his statement. Therefore, your claim that you said: "I know what it says in there," you only glanced at it and signed is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: You said that I left the room while Peric was reading. What if I tell you that we sat in the room, all the three of us, reading and signing together? Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I don't allow for that possibility. During the preparation of the interview and the taking of the statement, I thought about all options and decided against it. I knew that you and Mr. Peric were colleagues, that you knew each other well, that you may even exchange words in my absence, and I decided that you should read and sign your statement alone, only in my presence, whereafter Mr. Peric would do exactly the same, since he had already undertaken to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that the statement that I signed was perhaps clear to me, and if you read it out now to other people, it would not be so clear, it would not sound so clear?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when you were reading and signing the statement, what mattered to me was that it be clear to you. During my second visit, when I wanted you to sign the statement, I explained to you the purpose of my visit. I said that I had one copy, one hard copy, and one electronic copy on a floppy disk, that you need to review it, and if there is anything unclear, or if I misrecorded something due to the bad quality of the audio recording, we could make corrections. And after all that, when you said: "Yes, this is my statement. I can sign it," I understood that that statement is perfectly clear and logical to you and that is your testimony, and that I had recorded it perfectly, authentically, on paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: So you allow for the possibility that it was clear to me. Was it clear to you, though?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll have to listen to the audio recording. When you arrived at my office, and when we were talking, because the three of us were talking for quite a while before we proceeded to our statements, audio-recorded statements, do you remember how I approached that conversation? To be specific, do you remember that I asked you - excuse me - "Do you know in which humiliating way I was thrown out of the Defence room?" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know you mentioned it yesterday, but I really don't remember you mentioning that fact, being thrown out of the Defence room during the interview. I remember the conversation in that part which you mentioned yesterday, namely, that you understood we were to discuss one subject, why you were suspended, instead of two subjects.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: If I tell you now that I told you that I didn't understand why the attitude taken to me was the way it was and why I was suspended, somebody came to tell me that I had to leave the room and the security officer literally grabbed me by the shoulder and said: "You have to return your pass. You cannot be here any longer." And he escorted me out. Do you remember that I told you that?

utterances.speaker: DEJAN UKROPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that part of the conversation. I really don't. Maybe you mentioned it, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Maglov, I will let you ask as many questions as you like on that affair, but I honestly -- I have been trying to think about it since you raised it yesterday, but I honestly don't know how it's helping you in this case. Feel free to continue asking questions on what you refer to as your suspension, but where does it fit in in these proceedings? We're not discussing that. That's not before us. It was never before us in these proceedings, so -- and I frankly don't know how much it helps you to keep on mentioning this matter when others who are listening don't know anything about it. I don't know. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I raised this only for the reason that I asked the witness whether I was really upset, because for many months after this event I was unable to concentrate on anything. Whenever I started to explain this, I got so upset that when I tried to listen to my statement again, I didn't understand myself, I didn't understand what I had said. It leaps from one topic to another, it's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disjointed. I don't know when I'm discussing something we were talking about, when I was talking about something I'd said to the witness. That's the reason I raise this issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I fully understand that, Ms. Maglov. I mean, we have spent the last two days listening to witnesses that have been traumatised, and so we know exactly what it feels like when something has hit you, and hit you hard. So -- but again, it's up to you. If you want to continue asking questions on this event through the witness, do ask him, but we see absolutely no relevance except insofar that you now have explained that you were still emotionally disturbed by your suspension, by the fact of your suspense, and more particularly by the way you allege you were thrown out of the courtroom when you were approached by Mr. Ukropina. But otherwise, you're free to ask any questions you like. I was just trying to help you, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I must say that now, when I put a question to Mr. Ukropina, who worked as an amicus, a professional, and dealt with all the witnesses, and when he says what he did, does this show that people cannot really hang on to words at a particular moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One simply doesn't think, concentrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. No arguments in the presence of the witness, or criticism of the witness, or the way he is testifying, except in the form of asking him a question. But no argument. That's pleading, and we are -- we haven't arrived at --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you should apologise not to us but to him. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If possible, could we show the witness the conclusion on the basis of which he put before the Trial Chamber his arguments for an indictment on the count of intimidation?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Since at the beginning of these proceedings, respondent was asked if she had any challenges to the jurisdiction or the form of the pleadings, I would ask that it be made clear what the relevance of this line of questioning will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question. I mean, first, what are you -- what do you intend to ask the witness, Ms. Maglov, before you actually put the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only intend to ask him, in connection with count 1, whether it's usual for somebody who is a professional to make conclusions in this manner, whether this is the usual procedure, because there are no facts. That's why I want to put this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, that's -- you can legally ask him to repeat here in open court on what basis he came to that conclusion, which is a factual and legal conclusion, and you can put further questions to the witness to contest his reply to you, if that's the case, but not beyond that. I mean, it's -- he had been instructed, tasked, by the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin -- by us, by us three in the Brdjanin team, as amicus curiae, to go through the facts and report back to us whether there was a prima facie case to answer, and we specifically referred the amicus curiae to the relevant sections of -- the relevant Rule, Rule 77. He was tasked to report back to us on the basis of the facts that he established. I mean, we could basically disagree completely with him. But his role was to go through the facts, try to find out the facts, establish the facts, make an assessment of them, and on a prima facie basis, report back to us whether there was a prima facie case to answer. So if you believe that no lawyer or no amicus curiae could have come to that conclusion, you have every right to put the question to him and ask him how he came to that conclusion, but not beyond that. In other words, I'm trying to explain to you: If, in the mind of Mr. Ukropina, on a prima facie basis, the resulting facts amounted to intimidation, then his duty was to report back to us: Your Honours, there is a prima facie case to answer, in my opinion. But you have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- ask him: Don't you think that the facts were such that you couldn't have possibly come to that conclusion? You have every right to ask him. But you also have to point out why to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would take a very long time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take as much time as you like. We haven't put any time limits on either Prosecution or on you. Take as much time as you like, Ms. Maglov. This is -- this is your case, so we will protect your rights from beginning to end. So if you need two days, three days to cross-examine the witness, you will have two days, three days to cross-examine the witness. Because he's one of the key witnesses, obviously. I mean, you are here on the basis of -- because he filed a report which, to us, was acceptable, and on that basis, we ordered that proceedings be instituted against you. So you have every right to contest his conclusions if you want -- if you believe that you can do that. So go ahead. I will not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legal question that I am interested now is whether these conclusions are part of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The report is part of the case, but we are here to establish the facts ourselves now, okay? In other words, let me go back and you are a lawyer, and I will express it to you in legal terms. Had Mr. Ukropina, amicus curiae appointed by the Trial Chamber, come back to us and said, stated in his report: "Dear Judges, I have investigated the matter as instructed, as tasked by you. It is doubtful, in my mind, whether there is a prima facie case to answer. And this is my report. There is no prima facie case to answer." The matter would have stopped there. We would not have advanced it one single bit, because we did not task ourselves at the time to investigate it ourselves. We entrusted a lawyer, an amicus curiae, approved by the Registrar to do that for us. It so happened that after hearing evidence, taking statements, Mr. Ukropina came to the other conclusion, that in his calculated assessment, there was a prima facie case to answer, that you should answer a charge for intimidation and for having contravened, also violated an order not to -- I needn't go into detail. On the basis of that report, we instructed the issuance of -- or the institution of proceedings against you. Now, the report obviously forms part of the records, but our task now is to collect the evidence, and in the evidence also there is Mr. Ukropina's report, because it's part of the record, but it will be now our assessment, not Mr. Ukropina's assessment, which will decide whether you are guilty or not. And I don't think I need to explain this any further, because you sat in the Defence bench until a few months ago, or until a year ago, so you know exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I withdraw this question. Let me just explain why I put it. Evidently, I was wrong. While reading the Rules, I misunderstood who could be an amicus curiae. I thought they had to be experts, people with far more experience, and for these reasons, I obviously made a mistake. Thank you. What I wish now is to have the witness shown the decision on my suspension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but what's the relevance of this now? I have to ask you about the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision on my suspension deals with all the issues, to a far greater extent than it deals with this issue. First, it says that I was suspended because of a decision by the lead counsel, that there is a conflict of interest, that I violated the professional code, and only in passing is there mention of this point. That's why I wish this shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I cannot allow this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hollis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I also enter an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This amicus was tasked with the allegations here. This is not relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what exactly I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me try and explain this very clearly. Mr. Ukropina was never tasked to go into the matter of what led to your suspension from co-counsel as co-counsel in the Brdjanin and Talic case. If he even -- even if he -- if he even entertained for a moment or allowed himself to be involved in a discussion with you on the matter, both you and he made a mistake. It shouldn't have happened. That was never an issue. That was a decision of the Registrar, with which we, as Judges, do not -- had nothing to do and we don't interfere with. Mr. Ukropina was only tasked to investigate whether the allegation that the Prosecution submitted during the Brdjanin team, that you had intimidated a certain person, whose name cannot be mentioned here, was founded or unfounded. That was Mr. Ukropina's. The matter or the question or the possibility that that could have been taken into account while it was still an allegation by the Registrar in his decision to suspend you, it's irrelevant. It's not his business. It's not my business. It's not Judge Janu's or Judge Taya's business and it shouldn't be yours in these proceedings. What we are discussing is whether it's true or not now, on the basis of evidence we are hearing now, that there is a sufficient case proven by the Prosecution beyond reasonable doubt that you are indeed responsible for the crimes, for the offences with which you have been charged, but not beyond that. I am not going to allow this discussion or the cross-examination to go into matters that are completely unrelated and irrelevant to what we are discussing now. Please try to understand. It may well have been that the events that we are talking about, this alleged intimidation of the witness, formed part of the reasons why the Registrar decided to terminate your assignment as co-counsel. It could well be, but I am not interested in that. I'm not the Registrar, and I don't answer for the Registrar. What I'm interested in is whether the Prosecution in this case fulfils its task of proving beyond reasonable doubt your criminal responsibility. If it does, you will be found guilty and dealt with according to the Rules. If the Prosecution doesn't, you will be acquitted, and your acquittal will have absolutely no reflection at all on the previous incident which essentially formed the basis of the Registrar's decision. So why talk about it? I don't know. I hope I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to tender this decision on suspension as Exhibit number 4 because I said I wanted to testify before all other Defence witnesses. So if possible, I would like to tender it into evidence as D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still don't see the relevance of it, but I will let you tender it. But I want also to make it clear that I will not allow these proceedings to become a platform for you to deal with the matter of your suspension. We are not dealing with that. That is a matter that you can deal with -- or you had an opportunity to deal with directly with the Registrar or with the President of the Tribunal, if that was the case. Now we are dealing only with the alleged intimidation of the witness, whose name cannot be mentioned. That's all. And the violation of the order not to disclose the information, personally data of that witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that document should be marked D5, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions, because I see now how wrong I was in certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't -- is there a re-examination, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for you, Mr. Ukropina. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, of Judge Janu and Judge Taya and myself, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony. I had an occasion to thank you previously for your report. Now you have given evidence, which will be taken into account in our deliberations. You will be escorted by Madam Usher and you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return home at the earliest convenience. May I wish you, on behalf of everyone here, a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, yesterday I suggested to you that you only had one witness left, except that usually when I go to bed in the evening, my mind starts -- continues working. It takes some time before I unwind completely, and I remembered that you had also mentioned Ms. Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, she was mentioned as a potential witness if any issues came up as to disclosure. She is not a witness, and Mr. Ackerman would be my last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to calling in Mr. Ackerman, however, I do have a document I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On Monday, there was discussion about Prosecution Exhibit 4, which is the pre-trial Chamber order of 3 July 2000. And the discussion had to do with the translation of that order into B/C/S. And I believe the Court tasked the Registrar to determine if there had been a translation. In fact, there had been a translation of that order, and the Registrar has provided me with copies of the distribution sheet, showing distribution of what I am told is the B/C/S version of that order, and I would like to tender that distribution sheet into evidence. There does require some explanation, because it was not clear to me and I had to understand it from the court officer. The exhibit is a one-page registration distribution form. At the top of it is marked "D4376 ter." D4376 is the same designation as the distribution form for the decision itself. I am told the "ter" indicates this is in the B/C/S language. That is what I was informed by the registry. So I would like to offer this into evidence and to keep it a little tighter in terms of organisation, I'd like to offer it as 4.1, since that would relate it with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I have learned something new today. After two years here I have learned that "ter" means B/C/S. I didn't know that. I wasn't aware of that. Is there any objection on your part, Ms. Maglov, for the admission of this document? Well, I think it's logical follow-up of what we stated on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is so admitted. Shall we bring in Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher -- sorry. Okay. Take that first. In the meantime, Madam Registrar, if you could please contact Mr. Van de Vliet from the OLAD because he was supposed to report back to us on assignment of counsel today and I want to know where we stand. You know, we are nearing the end of the case and we haven't done anything as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Jevtovic, when there are technical requirements that you need to draw my attention to, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for thinking about it, but I think -- I believe strongly that we will finish before any technical requirements are needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find Mr. Ackerman? He is probably in the Defence room. He is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Here he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had already written half the contempt order, Mr. Ackerman, and it was giving me great pleasure going through it. Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more, I apologise to you that I told you yesterday probably your testimony would come up round about half 9.00. We are now 10.00. You know what the procedure is. Could I kindly ask you to enter the solemn -- make the solemn declaration, according to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a chair. Before we start the direct, I think I ought to explain to you, in particular, but also to Ms. Hollis and Ms. Maglov, how we intend to proceed. I'm fully aware that you are Defence -- lead Defence counsel in the Brdjanin team, in the Brdjanin case, from which these proceedings originate, and that respondent in this case was your co-counsel in the Brdjanin case and previously your investigator or legal assistant. I intend to take your examination question by question, and if at any time you believe, Mr. Ackerman, that you should not answer any question that is put to you because of any privilege that you may believe you have, then you ask us and we will decide whether it's the case of answering or not. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Ms. Hollis, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe we've established for the record, based on the earlier comments, that you are Mr. John Ackerman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that you are lead counsel for the Brdjanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long you have served as lead counsel for the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I was assigned in July or August of 2000. I'm not sure right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the respondent in this case has served with you as a legal assistant since 20 August 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if it's 1999, then I would have been assigned to the Brdjanin case in 1999 instead of 2000. And you're probably right. You've got the records there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to show you a series of exhibits and then ask you questions about those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if I could please ask that Exhibit P3 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, as you see, this is a 10 January 2000 Prosecution motion, with a Registry distribution form showing service on you on 10 January 2000.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you or anyone working with you or on your behalf provide a copy of this pleading, access to this pleading, or other notice of the contents of this pleading to respondent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when did that occur, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will both counsel kindly remember pauses between questions and answers. They speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard the interpreter. Please try to cooperate as much as you can. Their life is difficult behind those window panes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What practice would you have had in terms of providing such documents to respondent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The materials in this case were arriving at my office periodically in fairly large numbers. A document like this would have come by fax. All the documents that arrived in this case were put in a stack, in order of their arrival, processed by being given document numbers and scanned into an electronic system, and then copies of those documents were eventually, when they numbered somewhere between 300 and 500 pages, sent by DHL to my team in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you have retained those DHL receipts as to those mailings that you did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I probably have. I might have DHL bills that I paid that would show a number of shipments to Banja Luka, but it wouldn't identify the documents that went in those shipments.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So as I understand it, when you sent the materials would be based upon a page count, roughly; is that correct? When you reached a certain volume, you would send them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The cost of sending materials by DHL to Banja Luka is very high, and the Registry doesn't reimburse for it, and so I would wait until I got somewhere between 300 and 500 pages before I sent the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And would you have any estimate as to the time interval that it would take for you to have amassed that number of pages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, it would depend on the time of the case. Sometimes the document flow was much higher than other times. With regard to this particular document, I'd just be guessing, and I probably shouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course. Based on the practice that you had, do you think it is probable that you would have sent this document to respondent within one year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within six months?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask now that the witness be shown Exhibit P4 and P4.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As you see, this is the 3 July 2000 decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures and a Registry distribution form showing service on you on the 3rd of July of 2000. And sir, if I could draw your attention to page 25 of that decision, under the heading "disposition," number 1B of the orders in that decision, where it defines Brdjanin and Talic Defence team to mean only the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, and Momir Talic, and such Defence counsel and their immediate legal assistants and staff, and others specifically assigned by the Tribunal to Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic's Defence teams. And then, sir, if you could look at number 4 of those orders. "Save as is directly and specifically necessary for the preparation and presentation of this case, the Brdjanin and Talic Defence shall not disclose to the public the names identifying information or whereabouts of any witness or potential witness identified to them by the Prosecutor; b, any evidence, including documentary, physical, or other evidence, or any written statement of a witness or potential witness, or the substance, in whole or part, of any such non-public evidence, statement, or prior testimony." When did you, sir, or anyone working with you or on your behalf, provide respondent with a copy of, access to, or other notice of the contents of this decision?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Hollis, I couldn't begin to tell you the exact date. I know that it was sent to my office on 3 July. I know that that would have been -- that I probably wouldn't have been working that day because it would have been 4th of July holidays. I don't know when I came back to work after that. I do know when I scanned this document into my system.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was able to determine that, if I can look at a piece of paper here, I can tell you. It was scanned into my system on the 8th of August of 2000, the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And sir, if you will look at 4.1, which has been provided to you. This is a Registry distribution sheet showing service of the B/C/S version of this document, and we know the B/C/S version because the court officer indicated that the annotation "ter" up at the top, with the page number, indicates B/C/S, shows distribution to you on the 28th of July of 2000. Do you know when you would have scanned that into your system?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. August 15th, 2001. I don't know why. That "ter" may be the French version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I can only say what the court officer told me, and they said "ter" means B/C/S, as it's a tertiary or third language?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because they were rapidly doing the defence because of General Talic's Defence team in the French language. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Hollis. You replied August 15th, 2001. Is it 2001 or 2000, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's 2001, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 4th of July 2000 or 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was scanned August 8th of 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there an explanation why practically the same -- we're talking of practically the same document, one document was scanned a month later and another -- the other one a year and a month later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all I know is that the B/C/S versions of orders in this case frequently are not provided for a very long time. It takes a long time for them to get translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because this order imposed obligations on members of your team other than yourself, would you have taken measures to provide this order to respondent more quickly than was your normal practice?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've wondered about this question, Ms. Hollis, ever since it was clear that I would be a witness in this case, and I just don't know. I would think so, but I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in your estimate, this -- and you mentioned that you had scanned this in on the 8th of August of 2000. Was it your practice to scan it in before you sent materials or copies of materials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would be scanned in before it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if it had been scanned in on 8 August 2000, can you give this Court any estimate as to the time period which would have passed before you had sent this to the respondent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably not very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that, sir? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, a little while ago you said a year or six months, and I agreed with you that it certainly would be within six months, and I think probably less than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would it have been within three months?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think easily within three months. The volume of material that was coming would have made that almost certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now if I could ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, previously I just referred you to your privilege rights that might exist. There are other rights as well that you are aware of, should there be questions that could embarrass you and you would like not to answer, you can also do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, should that arise, we can certainly deal with that. I'm not aware that embarrassment is a privilege.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have used embarrassment, because Mr. Ackerman knows exactly what I am referring to. We have here Rules of -- there are the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. There is practice, legal practice that each lawyer adopts in his work, and there are also rules of conduct, plus an organisation, an association, which deals with those matters. So our Rules do not as such cover the -- in any detail the privilege rights that I referred to earlier, but I will not allow -- or I would entertain -- I would consider -- give serious consideration to any request that Mr. Ackerman would make regarding possible shortcomings that could expose him either to criticism by the association or censure by the association or whatever. Not that I think he has done that, because Mr. Ackerman, amongst all the lawyers that I have had to deal with in my life as a judge, stands foremost as one of the most precise. But anyway, let's not deal with that, and go ahead. If there are questions that he prefers -- he asks not to answer, we will discuss that and we will decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I am certainly not asking any questions to attempt to impugn his integrity. I am simply trying to get facts about service of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And sir, you have now Exhibit P5?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in this document, it shows service, it was filed on the 31st of July and served on you, I believe it shows, the 31st of July of 2000. This document sets out risk that exists to non-Serbs in certain areas who would testify against Serb accused. Did you or anyone working with you or on your behalf give a copy of, access to, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Hollis. I wouldn't like to have this answered in public session if it's going to refer to the area where the witness lived. So if you refrain from directing your question there, I will leave it in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I am being reminded actually that this document was exhibited under seal. So this is what I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: There were two such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P5. Let's stop for -- let's go into private session for a while. We'll decide accordingly whether to redact the previous part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the position, therefore, is as follows: As long as you follow the instructions that I gave you, in other words, not to make any direct reference to the municipality where the witness resided at the time, then we can remain into open session. If you need to refer to the municipality, then we will go into private session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I do not -- the general statement was simply to give a summary as to what the document was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's notice to you as well, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, again the same question: Did you or anyone working with you or on your behalf give a copy of, access to, or other notice of this document to respondent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is the same as with regard to the other documents. Yes. Every document that I received in this case was processed and sent to my staff in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this shows service on you on 31 July 2000. If we could again talk about possible time frames for when this would have been sent respondent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within what period of time do you believe this would have been sent to respondent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again I would just be guessing, but I would think three months or less. Probably a great deal less, but I have to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now if the witness could be shown Exhibit P6, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reminded that P6 is under seal, and P5 was also under seal. But in any case, we did not give any details on the document, so I see no harm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: For this we will, Your Honour, to some extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Is there cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I will have a very few questions, Your Honour, but after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break. Do you require a long break or a short break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not long. The usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a 25-minute break. And are you going to give -- are you going to bring forward any evidence today after Mr. Ackerman finishes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will discuss, Your Honour, and we will make a proposal and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we are going to have a short break, 25 minutes or so, and I hope -- we hope we finish with you immediately after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Can you explain to the Court what the duties of the members of your Defence team are. You were the lead counsel. What were the duties of the others?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there were a number. Primarily, what I relied on with regard to the Banja Luka team was to conduct investigations into the allegations against our client, Mr. Brdjanin, for translation and interpretation services, for providing me with the benefit of that team's knowledge and experience with regard to the various documents and materials that were being provided by the Prosecution and forwarded to Banja Luka. I don't know that I can go much further in that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: With respect to Court decisions, did we, as the other members of the team, rely on you to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand your question. The primary responsibility in responding to Prosecution motions and filing motions on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin and any other necessary filings with the Court were my responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that answer, Mr. Ackerman, but I myself was a little bit confused with the question. The question did not refer to responding to Prosecution motions and filing motions on behalf of your client, and other necessary filings. But what Ms. Maglov referred to in her question to you was: "With respect to Court decisions, did we, as the other members of the team, rely on you to deal with that?" I myself don't understand the question. Perhaps Ms. Maglov can rephrase it or it could be a question of interpretation. I don't know. But we're dealing with decisions, it's one thing; if we're dealing with motions and responses to motions, answering, replying to motions, that's another. So can I ask you, Ms. Maglov, to be kind enough to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: As this was an extensive case and we had many documents, witness statements, over 220, I think, was it an implicit rule that we would deal with those documents and responding to Court decisions was the task of the lead counsel, we, as members of the team, did not have time to study Court decisions. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, one moment. I don't expect Mr. Ackerman to answer for you, I mean, whether you had enough time -- anyway, I leave you free, Mr. Ackerman, to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect to this Trial Chamber, I must refuse to answer this question on the grounds that it calls for disclosure of protected attorney work product information and that it calls for disclosure of oral or written communications by and between members of the Brdjanin Defence team made in anticipation of or during trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your position on that, Ms. Hollis? I have here a compendium of decisions, including decisions from Texas, Houston, Mr. Ackerman, and from the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia. So I'm prepared on this matter. What's your position on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, first of all, invoking work product, of course, is not a magic incantation, and the extent to which work product would apply would depend on the type of communication that is being asked about. The Prosecution's position on this would be that in regard to -- if -- and again, I don't really understand what the respondent is asking. But if the respondent were asking something to the effect: Did you prioritise for us what decisions we should have read, without going into why or whatever purposes that would serve, our position would be he could answer yes or no, I did. If the question were: "Did you ever tell us that we could ignore Court decisions imposing obligations on us?" The Prosecution would also submit that that question could be answered, because you cannot, as a matter of work product, refuse to answer which in effect would be telling people in your team to disobey a Court order. So without really knowing what she is going at, that would be my general position. If the communication goes to tactics that are to be used, to strategies that are to be used, to how evidence is to be analysed, to advice that is to be given, to evaluations of different positions, all of that would be protected by work product. So unless there's a specific question directed, I'm not even sure that that -- that there can be a determination as to whether it's covered or not and I don't know what the specific question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My first reaction is this: Ms. Maglov, do you insist on your question, in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I don't insist on this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question has been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have other questions to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: All the documents shown to you today have been in English; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: With respect to Court documents, did you scan each and every one of them into your system? I'm referring to all the Court decisions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I scanned everything, but with the exception of some B/C/S translations, which I didn't scan, with regard to Court decisions, and French translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: I was about to ask about that, but you've already answered it. So when you receive a Court decision in B/C/S, you don't really understand the language; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: If I say that decisions in B/C/S were delivered by you, or rather, forwarded mostly to your client, would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Both. They were sent both to Banja Luka and delivered to Mr. Brdjanin at times when I would visit with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: My next question is: As documents were being sent electronically, were the documents that were in the electronic system in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It depends on the documents you're talking about. Some were, some weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I had to confer with Ms. Jevtovic, as she was the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. Take your time, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: Initially, we received all the documents in hard copies. Later on, we switched over to the electronic format. With regard to these decisions, what was the technology of their delivery?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask Ms. Jevtovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to specify which decisions you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you are aware of what documents are in this case, but Mr. Ackerman doesn't. I mean, I suppose she is referring to the decisions that form part of the records of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman wasn't here when Ms. Hollis was tendering these in evidence, so we need to explain to Mr. Ackerman what we are talking about. And not all exhibits are decisions, Ms. Maglov, so I would kindly ask you to go through --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I'm now referring to the Brdjanin case, not this case. I'm asking about the way we operated in the Brdjanin case and about the flow of information between Mr. Ackerman and the Defence team in the Brdjanin case, not this present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To the electronic -- the ones which were delivered in electronic format or the ones which were delivered in hard copies?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. So let's start with the documents that, in the initial period, according to Ms. Maglov, you used to send to Banja Luka in hard copies. What was the procedure that was followed, or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as it was put, the technology of the delivery, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I explained earlier in my testimony that the documents would come into my office by courier from the Office of the Prosecutor, by fax from the Registry. I would give them identification numbers, I would scan them into my system, I would then send copies of those documents by DHL to Banja Luka, when I got a number somewhere between 300 and 500 of them. There came a time when, instead of, and primarily for two reasons: The cost of delivery by DHL is very high; and second, the technology developed in Banja Luka so that we could put together a system there that would permit the searching of the documents, the searching of the materials. And so I then began delivering the materials in electronic format in a couple of different ways, as I recall, but I don't remember when I switched over to the electronic format. There was also a time when we switched from the Adobe Acrobat format to the ZyLAB format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that cover your question, Ms. Maglov, or do you want more information?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, the gentleman replied that he couldn't be certain as to when we started receiving documents in electronic format. But we switched over to the electronic format quite quickly. Can the witness confirm this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, with regard to the documents that were filed with the Registry, the motions, the pleadings, the indictment, all of those things, that those were supplied electronically very early on in Adobe Acrobat format. The Prosecution's disclosure of potential exhibits and witness statements I think was in hard copy for a much longer period of time. I think there were several shipments of 500 pages, roughly, to Banja Luka, maybe as many as ten such shipments before we switched to full electronic. But I don't recall. It's been too long.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. We shall have our own witnesses to testify about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you've finished with Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the respondent asked you about duties of teams, and you talked about duties of the Banja Luka team. Earlier in this hearing, Ms. Jevtovic indicated she joined the Brdjanin team initially in August 1999, firstly as an interpreter and then as an investigator. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't remember when titles changed and things like that. I think it was about that time that she joined the team, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And was she assigned to the Banja Luka team?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there came a time when you did begin to deliver documents or information in an electronic format and that you believe that you began to do this fairly quickly with documents that were filed with the Registry, and that would have included the 3 July 2000 decision, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they -- I know they were furnished both ways, both hard copy and electronically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And do you know if you sent that electronically?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that requires, I guess, a little bit of explanation. When I say furnished electronically, a file was maintained on my computer in Texas of every filing that came from the Registry, in a particular file. Occasionally, that entire file would be put on a CD-ROM or some other electronic media and shipped by DHL or carried by me to Banja Luka and furnished to the team there. So what that means is the early documents in the case were probably delivered dozens of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was just -- it was being upgraded each time I would send that file, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when earlier they spoke about changing the method of providing them information and doing it electronically, what you're saying, as I understand it, is that you did not actually transmit it to them electronically; you put it on a CD and then would have it delivered by more traditional means, either DHL or some other means; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, except there were occasions when I would deliver something by attachment to e-mail if I thought it was particularly important.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And would that have been the case with this 3 July 2000 decision?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea. Probably not, because I think the capabilities in Banja Luka were not up to that level yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That early.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there are no questions from the Bench. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I should like to thank you for having come over, for having patiently waited, I don't know how long, yesterday, and once more this morning. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that conclude the case for the Prosecution, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask the court deputy to clarify one matter that was raised during Mr. Ackerman's testimony, then my case would be concluded. If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead. Ms. Chen, when you provided me the distribution sheet for the 3 July 2000 decision with the annotation on that sheet of D4376 ter, is it correct that the designation "ter" indicates that the decision was being distributed in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, and also filed in B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the French version, would it be bis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the English, nothing? All right. So I take it that the case for the Prosecution stands here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which means the ball is in your court, Ms. Maglov, now. And the first thing I am going to ask you is whether you intend to offer your testimony, in which case, whether you are going to testify now. Do you require more time to think about this? Because it seems that you were not quite sure until the break. And then, obviously, whether you have any witnesses. And we'll take it up from there. Ms. Maglov. You have a right to remain silent, of course. You know that, that no one can force you to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Rules to be applied to these proceedings are from 4 to 8, mutatis mutandis. According to Rule 98 bis, after having heard and seen all the Prosecution evidence, I want, under Rule 98 bis, to move for an acquittal before adducing the Defence evidence pursuant to Rule 85(A)(i). I may submit this either in writing or orally, and I believe that in this way we can save time. As far as I have been able to study the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, I have seen that in the jurisprudence, motions for acquittal have always been considered after the Prosecution case, and the standard applied was lower than the standard of beyond reasonable doubt. The test for such a motion was formulated by the Trial Chamber, asking whether there is evidence that the Chamber would accept that would legally support a finding of guilty. For example, in the Tadic case, and in some other cases, this has been explained in similar terms. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, as I explained earlier on, there is a Rule which specifies that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence applicable to the normal trials that we have here apply, mutatis mutandis, also to contempt proceedings. You have, of course, every right to invoke the application of Rule 98 bis. Therefore, these proceedings are adjourned for a decision by the Trial Chamber on that matter. Basically, this also means that I will now, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, fix a time limit for the filing of the Rule 98 bis motion, and of course there will be a time limit fixed, for you, Ms. Hollis, to respond. I take it that you are not going to file an ad hoc motion for the application of Rule 98 within the seven days contemplated in Rule 98 bis, because you've made an oral request. All right. So I am giving you -- how much time do you require, Ms. Maglov, for your submissions in support of your Rule 98 bis motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect I may be able to submit this motion on Monday, if that is not too late, or maybe even earlier. I would like to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking, instead of fixing the time arbitrarily, without asking you, I'm asking you how much time you require, and provided the time you indicate to us is a reasonable one, we will meet your requirements. So how much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I need too much time, but I think that by Monday I could make the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Trial Chamber is granting you a week within which to file the supporting material, or your statement in support of -- your submissions in support of your Rule 98 bis motion. How much time would you require? Obviously, you're going to tell me I haven't seen the document as yet. Would another week suffice, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't exactly what I was going to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I can begin work on this issue immediately, because I understand what my obligation is. I would then need just a short period of time to read the motion and see if what I have prepared responds to it appropriately. So I think once I receive the motion, it shouldn't take me more than a day or two to have finalised my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll do it this way: We have granted Ms. Maglov one week. She can utilise the whole period. She can file her motion by Monday if she prefers to do that. We will also give you one week from service of Ms. Maglov's document, and of course you can utilise the entire week or you can file your response earlier. We would then require our time to go into the matter ourselves. That basically means that immediately after you have filed this motion -- or you can actually return to Banja Luka now if you want, because you can file it electronically or you can file it by fax. You don't need to be present here in The Hague to file this motion. But if you do so, please inform Ms. Hollis, in particular, that you are no longer in The Hague. That's the other point. And then we will communicate with you the date when we expect to hand down our Rule 98 bis decision and we will move from there according to what the decision will be. In the meantime, I think it is your duty, Ms. Maglov, especially since you asked us earlier on to issue a summons, a subpoena, vis-a-vis one of your witnesses, Mr. Peric, to inform him that his presence in The Hague on Monday will no longer be required. And I'm going to instruct Registrar to take that into consideration and to act accordingly. But since he's your witness and also your partner, I suggest that you do that straight away. Yes, Ms. Maglov.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stay, because I intend to submit the motion on Monday. I would like to use the library, and I ask that either I or my assistant be given a badge so that we can use the library. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, please take note of that. I know that it's not within my power or our power to grant that permission, but I'm sure that the Registrar will know exactly what to do. So is there anything else before we rise? Yes, Ms. Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Regarding the request made by Ms. Maglov, I would like to inform Your Honours that we have -- we got the badges which allow us to access the Defence room, the courtrooms, the library, the cafeteria, et cetera, only for seven days, and I would like Your Honours to instruct -- I don't understand why this happened. Normally, the Registry, the OLAD office, issues the badges for the Defence attorneys for a period of six months. Why was it different in this case? Because this case is not over yet, and we don't know as of today how long it's going to last. So I would really like Your Honours to look into this, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Jevtovic, I think it's clear enough. First of all, I think the pass was granted to you even before you were approved as legal assistant, or more or less at the same time. That's number one. And with regard to Ms. Maglov, I think she has a dual personality here. She is a lawyer and she is an accused defending herself. So I think I cannot speak for the Registrar and say exactly what the procedure to be adopted should be. I think the Registrar knows exactly how to proceed in these matters, and honestly, although I see the utility of being able to have access to the library, particularly as far as you are concerned, as legal assistant, I would prefer not to pronounce myself with regard to your mother's position. So I think I would leave it entirely to the Registrar. I'm sure that Madam Registrar here will communicate the gist of this discussion, this debate, to the Registrar, and I'm sure that the Registrar will be reasonable as he usually is. But I cannot instruct the Registrar what to do and which passes to grant and to whom and for how long and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. Thank you very much. I just wanted to inform you on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we rise, I think is Mr. Van de Vliet still outside the courtroom? Yes, could we call Mr. Van de Vliet, please? I did make enquiries actually what the position was with regard to the assignment of counsel, but just for formality's sake, I know that you also have been informally informed of what the position is, or would likely to be at the end of today. Mr. Van de Vliet, good morning to you, and thank you for having been patient with us waiting outside the courtroom for more than half an hour. I would like you to report back to the Trial Chamber on the respondent's request for assignment of counsel under the legal aid system. MR. VAN de VLIET: Good morning, Your Honours. The Registrar has looked into the declaration of means which was submitted by the accused in this case, and has made a comparison to the scope of these proceedings and made an estimation of that. In light of all that, we think that the person is not indigent, which means she should be able to pay the costs of this proceeding herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Yes, one further question: This is -- does this mean that a decision has been formalised? MR. VAN de VLIET: Yes, we have a decision ready. It's now probably at this moment being filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you, Mr. Van de Vliet. So you know what are your rights, Ms. Maglov. If you want to contest the substance of this decision. And there will be ample time for that, because obviously we are going to have the interval of time to deal with the Rule 98 bis motion, which you can make avail of, you can avail yourself of. All right. Thank you, Mr. Van de Vliet. So we rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAGLOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We rise and we will meet again, should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it be the case, after the decision, our decision on the Rule 98 bis. Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.34 a.m.,
